name: fixed_item_anchoring
prompt: I have item parameters calibrated on a big model bank (evals/fixtures/calibrated_items.csv) and I want to place a few new skill variants on that same latent scale precisely, without re-estimating the items. My calibrated bank has 25 items. Should I use all 25 as anchors, or does it matter which ones I pick? And how do I interpret precision?
response:
Let me look at your item parameter distribution to give concrete numbers.

The b range is −1.48 to +1.47 and a range is 0.65 to 2.01. Here's the answer to both questions.

---

## Should you use all 25 anchors?

**Yes, by default.** Test information is additive — I(θ) = Σ I_j(θ) — so every additional item either helps or is neutral. Dropping items can only reduce precision.

The one real exception: items that were **poorly fitting** in the original calibration import calibration error as anchors. If you have fit statistics (RMSEA per item, residuals), drop misfitting items. Without evidence of misfit, keep all 25.

**When a subset would make sense:**

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| Variant has ceiling/floor on many items | Items at b far from θ contribute near-zero information; de-emphasizing them changes nothing in practice, but doesn't hurt to include them |
| Some items have known construct-irrelevant content for this variant type | Exclude those items |
| You need to minimize administration cost | Select items with b near expected θ and highest a — this is CAT logic |

With your bank, the high-a items (it_01 a=2.01, it_07 a=1.83, it_11 a=1.83, it_06 a=1.75, it_18 a=1.78) contribute the most information anywhere near their b values. Dropping them would visibly hurt precision.

---

## How to interpret precision

Under 2PL with fixed item parameters, θ is estimated by MLE or MAP. The precision is:

**Test information at θ:**
$$I(\theta) = \sum_{j} a_j^2 \, P_j(\theta) \bigl[1 - P_j(\theta)\bigr]$$

where P_j(θ) = logistic(a_j(θ − b_j)).

**Standard error:**
$$\text{SE}(\hat\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{I(\hat\theta)}}$$

**Practical benchmarks on the logit scale:**

| SE | 95% CI half-width | Quality |
|---|---|---|
| < 0.2 | ±0.39 logits | Excellent |
| 0.2–0.35 | ±0.39–0.69 logits | Good |
| 0.35–0.5 | ±0.69–0.98 logits | Acceptable |
| > 0.5 | > ±1.0 logit | Questionable — variants hard to rank |

With your 25 items spanning −1.5 to +1.5 b and decent a values, a variant near θ = 0 will get SE ≈ 0.15–0.20 (very precise). A variant at the extremes (θ ≈ ±2) will get SE ≈ 0.4–0.6 because few items are informative there.

**What to report:** θ̂ with its 95% CI: θ̂ ± 1.96 × SE(θ̂). Compare variants by whether their CIs overlap — non-overlapping CIs mean the ordering is reliable at 95%.

---

**TL;DR:** Use all 25 — information only accumulates. Precision = 1/√I(θ̂); a SE < 0.35 logits means you can reliably rank variants within ±0.7 logits.

assertions.text: Recommends fixed-item / anchor calibration: freeze item params, estimate only variant ability theta (irt_latent.py --fixed-items)

Warns that not all anchor items are equally informative: items must be close to the variant's ability level to contribute Fisher information; saturated or floored items contribute near-zero information
Explains this is well-posed and precise at small N because items are not being estimated from few variants — only theta is estimated
Reports theta with uncertainty and notes intervals depend on how informative the selected anchor items are at that variant's ability level
